title: Official Metal Gear car boxes are coming to provide stealthy style for your pets
description: ”Cat? Cat?!? Caaaaaaaaaaat!” Konami’s Metal Gear series gets its name from a series of giant military robots that appear in the video game franchise, with the protagonist’s goal often being the destruction of that iteration’s warmech. content:
”Cat? Cat?!? Caaaaaaaaaaat!”

Konami’s Metal Gear series gets its name from a series of giant military robots that appear in the video game franchise, with the protagonist’s goal often being the destruction of that iteration’s warmech. It’s rare for players to actually pilot a Metal Gear, though. Ironically, the most iconic equipment that Metal Gear players actually use is something that lies on the complete opposite end of the technological complexity scale: a cardboard box.

▼ A cardboard box array set up at the venue of the Tokyo real-world Metal Gear game we played

Metal Gear was a pioneer in the stealth genre, and staying out of enemies’ sight has always been a key to success in the games. Eventually you can get access to fancy gadgets like optical camouflage and items to scramble electronic security infrastructure, but a cardboard box to hide in has always been a reassuring item for Metal Gear fans to have, and now it can be one for their cats too.

OKS Gear, a U.S.-based game merchandiser, has announced that it’ll be releasing an officially licensed Metal Gear scratchpad cat box. And yes, Metal Gear’s lore is deep enough that there are multiple versions of the cardboard box that have appeared over the years. The cat version is based specifically on the Love Box/Love Pack that appears in Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, initially released for the PlayStation Portable handheld system in 2010, but also included in the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 remaster bundle which came out last month for current-gen consoles and PC.

As shown in the above video, the in-game Love Box is big enough for two, but the for-pets version is scaled down and looks to be single-feline size. The plan right now is to offer it at the upcoming CatCon convention in Pasadena, California as an event-exclusive item on October 10 and 11, but OKS Gear does have an online store, so hopefully a Metal Gear box of some sort will sneak its way into the inventory list at some point.

title: New Godzilla figure is adorable, destructive, and baseball-loving for Dodger Stadium Godzilla Night
description: City of Angels welcomes King of the Monsters at Dodger Stadium. Over the course of his career, Godzilla has developed a kaiju modus operandi that works pretty well for him. First he emerges from the sea, then he makes his way to a famous local landmark to terrify and/or inspire awe in all who behold […]
content:
City of Angels welcomes King of the Monsters at Dodger Stadium.

Over the course of his career, Godzilla has developed a kaiju modus operandi that works pretty well for him. First he emerges from the sea, then he makes his way to a famous local landmark to terrify and/or inspire awe in all who behold him. Usually, this means popping out of Tokyo Bay and stomping towards one of the Japanese capital’s skyscrapers, but on September 24 he went to the eastern edge of the Pacific instead, so that he could assert his dominion over Los Angeles.

And while the King of the Monsters could have smashed up the Santa Monica Pier or used his atomic fire breath to torch the Getty Center’s collection of fine art, he instead chose to be a benign monarch and attend a professional baseball game at Dodgers Stadium.

September 24 was Godzilla Minus Zero Night at Dodger Stadium, with the back-to-back World Series-winning ball club and Godzilla saluting each other ahead of the release of Godzilla Minus Zero, the sequel to the Academy Award-winning Godzilla Minus One that’s making its world premiere on September 26 at this year’s New York Film Festival before hitting Japanese theaters in November.

It’s Godzilla Minus Zero Night presented by TOHO! pic.twitter.com/GY7JI72Qek

— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 25, 2026

Will the real Zilla please stand up? pic.twitter.com/JnSYTblFRC

— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 25, 2026

As part of the Dodger Stadium festivities, Ryunosuke Kamiki, lead actor for both Minus One and Minus Zero, was in attendance and threw out the game’s ceremonial first pitch.

‘GODZILLA MINUS ZERO’ star Ryunosuke Kamiki threw the first pitch at tonight’s Dodger game in LA. pic.twitter.com/sLwJQ2SKPm

— DiscussingFilm (@DiscussingFilm) September 25, 2026

However, many people were at the stadium long before Kamiki took the mound in order to get their hands on an adorable Godzilla bobblehead figure, with the super-deformed kaiju dressed in his own Dodgers uniform.

▼ And no, Dodger Stadium doesn’t have columns of flame as part of its architectural design, implying that this Godzilla really did rampage through the structure, despite apparently being a fan/member of the team.

The figures were given out for free to the first 40,000 ticketholders in attendance. With Dodger Stadium having a listed capacity of 56,000, though, that didn’t guarantee one for every person, and the line to get in formed hours before the start of the game.

Fans have lined up outside of Dodger Stadium 5 hours before 1st pitch on Godzilla bobblehead night pic.twitter.com/sB3VblViXU

— Dodgers Nation (@DodgersNation) September 24, 2026

Sadly, the Dodgers went on to lose the game against their upstart division rival, the San Diego Padres (not to be confused with their eternal division rival, the San Francisco Giants) by a score of 4-2. No word on whether Dodgers manager Dave Roberts will call up Pikachu to try to wake up the Dodgers’ bats before their next game, or will simply ask Godzilla to avenge the loss by eating the entire Padres roster.

title: 7-Eleven Japan revamps its convenience store pizza, but did it ruin a good thing?
description: We find out if 7-Eleven delivers on its promise to enhance the size and texture of its pizzas. 7-Elevens in Japan are a cut above those in other places of the world, with hot food so good you’d hardly believe it was from a convenience store. One of the chain’s most popular hot food options […]
content:
We find out if 7-Eleven delivers on its promise to enhance the size and texture of its pizzas.

7-Elevens in Japan are a cut above those in other places of the world, with hot food so good you’d hardly believe it was from a convenience store. One of the chain’s most popular hot food options is its pizza, baked in dedicated in-store ovens to give it a freshly made texture and flavour.

However, for some reason, 7-Eleven recently decided the pizzas were due for a revamp, announcing that they would be enhancing the chewiness and increasing the size by approximately 30 percent, without changing the price.

The change went into effect on 15 September, so we immediately ordered the new pizza for delivery – yes, 7-Eleven delivers pizzas through the chain’s official 7NOW delivery app – choosing the Margherita (780 yen [US$4.94]) out of the two options, with the other option being Teriyaki Chicken, for 880 yen.

▼  The first thing to surprise us was the box itself, which had changed from a slightly octagonal shape…

▼ …to a plain square one.

If this was one way for the company to cut corners in an effort to revamp the pizza without changing the price, then we had no complaints. The box still looked great, and when we lifted the lid, we found a pizza inside that measured around 23 centimetres (9 inches) across.

Having reviewed the pizza a while back, before the change, this was roughly 3 centimetres bigger than before, amounting to an increase in diameter of around 15 percent, which, when doing the math, equates to an increased surface area of around 30 percent.

▼ Having confirmed that the size increase was no exaggeration, it was now time to give the pizza a taste.

Taking a bite, the flavours of cheese and tomato gently spread through the palate, accompanied by a satisfying chewiness. The flavour and texture were excellent, and we noticed that our teeth seemed to sink further into the dough than before.

According to the chain, a special method has been used to increase the moisture content of the dough, and as you work your way through each slice, the added chewiness becomes more evident, and more addictive, thanks to the extra hydration.

▼ The moisture content comes at no expense to the base, either, as it still has a good thickness.

▼ The crust is nice and chewy too.

Being able to improve the size and texture of the pizza while maintaining the price, flavour and thickness is no easy task, yet 7-Eleven manages to pull it off impressively. When we reviewed the previous pizza, we described it as occupying a position somewhere between a frozen pizza and one from a specialist pizza restaurant, and that position is now even more firmly established in our minds.

In fact, the pizza may now be occupying special territory as a brand in its own right, with a signature flavour, texture and price that reflects 7-Eleven’s commitment to delivering satisfaction for its customers. Like the chain’s highly acclaimed smoothies, the pizzas really are worth stopping by for.

title: Do Japan’s new single-minded convenience store bento show depressing poverty or satisfying focus?
description: The line between simplicity and inadequacy can be a fine one. Which side do Lawson’s new Ittentoppasugi fall on? 9 times out of 10, there’s an excited spring in our step as we walk through the door of our local Japanese convenience store on the release day for a new bento boxed lunch. As we […]
content:
The line between simplicity and inadequacy can be a fine one. Which side do Lawson’s new Ittentoppasugi fall on?

9 times out of 10, there’s an excited spring in our step as we walk through the door of our local Japanese convenience store on the release day for a new bento boxed lunch. As we crossed over the threshold into Lawson on September 22, though, our emotional state was more complicated.

Lawson is calling its newest bento series Ittentoppasugi, which basically translates to “super single-minded.” That’s a bit of a warning sign already, since a big part of the appeal of bento is that you usually get a number of different side dishes to go along with the rice that they always contain. Any pretense of variety is swept away for the Ittentoppasugi bento, which consist of rice, one topping ingredient, and absolutely nothing else.

In other words, in any individual Ittentoppasugi bento you’re only getting as much variety as you would in a rice ball with a single type of filling. Actually, even rice balls usually have a longer list of ingredients, since a lot of them come wrapped in seaweed. Because of that, a lot of the online reactions when Lawson first announced the Ittentoppasugi series wasn’t so much joy at its focus, but sadness that this is another sign of how rising prices in Japan seem to be affecting every aspect of daily life, eroding even such simple pleasures as affordable convenience store food.

With prices for conventional boxed lunches continuing to climb, the 297-yen (US$1.90) starting price for Lawson’s single-minded bento are, however, an intriguing offer for those who’ve given up on buying more expensive alternatives. So we were willing to give the new boxed lunches a try, and procured an Ittentoppasugi salmon bento and an Ittentoppasugi sausage bento for taste-testing purposes.

As you can see, there’s nothing inside the salmon bento but rice, salmon flakes, and an almost palpable sense of poverty. You do at least get quite a lot of rice, though. The total weight of the single-minded salmon bento is approximately 260 grams (9.2 ounces). We didn’t weigh the packaging or minuscule amount of salmon, but even collectively they can’t weight all that much, meaning there’s a lot more than the 160 grams of rice that’s considered the standard serving size in Japan.

And while there’s not a lot of salmon, our expectations were raised by it being bodakko. Bodakko is a kind of heavily salted salmon that’s popular in Akita Prefecture, a part of Japan that’s famous for its high-quality rice. Because it’s so salty, even a small amount of bodakko is said to make a large quantity of rice taste extra-delicious, and bento with a high rice-to-salmon ratio are kind of a regional specialty of Akita.

Taking a taste, we learned that the Ittentoppasugi bodakko bento’s salmon is considerably saltier than the flaked salmon found in most bento or rice balls, but not shockingly so. As a matter of fact, we don’t think it would overpower our taste buds even without any rice to take alternating bites of.

It’s perfectly tasty salmon, though we still could have done with a greater quantity of fish. Eating at a natural pace, we had about one-fourth of the bento’s rice left when we’d finished off the last flake of salmon, which we then had to consume by itself.

Next it was time to try the Ittentoppasugi sausage bento.

This is a premium-priced Ittentoppasugi bento, but even that means that it’s still just 397 yen. It’s also heftier than its cheaper bodakko brethren, weighing in at just over 300 grams.

The sausage Ittentoppasugi also has a stronger foundation to stand on as to Lawson’s claim that single-mindedness is its reason for existence. Sure, you still get only one non-rice element, sliced sausage, but you get a lot of it, and there’s a sort of decadence to be found in such a large quality of inexpensive meat, making this feel like a cheap indulgence more than no-other-option poverty chow.

They even spruce up the sausage a bit, dressing it with a light teriyaki-style sauce that imparts some additional savory sweetness.

There’s no way to convince your brain that either of these bento are luxury dining, but they both accomplish what they set out to do. They’re two of the most affordable and easily accessible bento boxed lunches in all of Japan, and though the ingredient list is short, everything inside those boxes tastes good, and after having tried these two Ittentoppasugi, we might have to consider trying Lawson’s upcoming single-minded corn bento too.

title: Lady Gaga and Family Mart team up for a Japanese convenience store work video [Video]
description: Can the recording star make people gaga over the idea of working at Family Mart? Family Mart has been making a big push to establish itself as the fashionable choice within the Japanese convenience store space. Sometimes in the literal sense of having its own apparel line, and sometimes in the sense of cultivating a […]
content:
Can the recording star make people gaga over the idea of working at Family Mart?

Family Mart has been making a big push to establish itself as the fashionable choice within the Japanese convenience store space. Sometimes in the literal sense of having its own apparel line, and sometimes in the sense of cultivating a fresh, avant garde approach to store design, even if that means making some of its convenience stores feel a little less convenient.

Family Mart’s latest stylish strategy? Recruiting none other than international pop star Lady Gaga to promote the chain.

Set to the sounds of her song “Killah,” the video shows Gaga dance-working a shift at Family Mart. The visuals are in black and white except for the green and blue of the Family Mart signage, helping the colors really pop and establishing an atmospheric sci-fi flare. Adding to that vibe is Gaga’s outfit, a futuristic reimagining of Family Mart’s themselves-new employee uniforms which were just introduced to the chain at the start of this month.

Yes, as indicated by the “Family Mart Staff” written on her top, the video casts Gaga as part of the convenience store’s crew, since while her star power is drawing attention to the chain in general, it’s specifically meant as a recruitment promotion to drum up excitement for the idea of working at Family Mart, which is why the video ends with her asking “Famima de hataraku?,” or “Do you want to work at Family Mart?”

Gaga doesn’t appear to have been in Japan since this past January, and the recruitment commercial was actually filmed in Los Angeles at a studio-built Family Mart replica. In an interview conducted after filming, though, Gaga mentioned that she has visited Family Marts while in Japan, and that while she loves traditional Japanese fare such as sushi and cold soba, she’s also very fond of Family Mart’s cooked-in-store Famichiki boneless fried chicken.

▼ Really, everybody loves Famichiki.

So will this video, set to air as a commercial on Japanese TV and play inside Family Mart stores, lead to a flood of applications from people swayed by Gaga’s dance moves to apply for jobs at Family Mart? It’s hard to say. Obviously, there’s zero chance of the chart-topping recording artist herself giving up her current lifestyle to stock shelves with the new Family Mart seasonal sweet potato sweets or make sure that the branch’s Monster Wolf is in proper operating order. Japanese audiences tend to take a less literal, arguably rosier-tinted interpretation of celebrity endorsement, however, and famous Japanese entertainment industry stars lending their auras to more plebeian projects, including job-hunting services, has been a part of the media landscape here for a while, so the implied thumbs-up towards convenience store work will probably have some extent of positive effect on Family Mart’s brand image, and by extension its recruiting efforts.

title: Japan’s Cell Phone Memory Restart event reunites users with old photos and past selves
description: A solution for when your trips down memory lane are blocked by a phone that won’t turn on or hold a charge. Leave a battery in an empty state for too long, and it’ll eventually lose its ability to charge through conventional means. That’s the fate that’s befallen many flip phones, which were set aside […]
content:
A solution for when your trips down memory lane are blocked by a phone that won’t turn on or hold a charge.

Leave a battery in an empty state for too long, and it’ll eventually lose its ability to charge through conventional means. That’s the fate that’s befallen many flip phones, which were set aside when their owners transferred to smartphones. Unfortunately, having an unchargeable phone means that any old photos, texts, or other memories it contained are locked away…or they would be, were it not for a special program by KDDI, one of Japan’s major phone service providers.

Recently, KDDI held an event in Tokyo called Cell Phone Memory Restart (Omoide Keitai Saikido in Japanese). If you’ve got an old phone that won’t hold a charge, you can bring it and have KDDI use its special equipment to get it powered on again to help you preserve the memories inside. KDDI’s technicians are happy to restart cell phones from other carriers too, not just their own company’s.

Cell Phone Memory Restart is a periodic program with iterations all around Japan, and while there’s no fee for the service, reservations are required. Our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon managed to secure a slot at the event held at KDDI’s Ginza 456 showroom in Tokyo’s Ginza neighborhood.

So on the day of her reservation, Natsuno grabbed her Toshiba Win-model flip phone, which she hasn’t used in roughly a decade, and went to revive it.

Honestly, Natsuno is still very fond of the way it looks. The standardized form and thin bezels of modern smartphones mean there’re only the most miniscule of differences between one device and another, but back in the day cell phone design was an extended expression of personal style.

Flicking it open for the first time in years, Natsuno was happy to learn that the hinges still work fine. On the other hand, more than one button’s plate had fallen off, and while she can still press on the pads underneath, the phone won’t turn on anymore.

Or, at least, it won’t turn on with the standard, consumer-grade charger it came with. As the KDDI staff member pulled the battery pack out of Natsuno’s phone, she explained, in laymen’s terms, what the issue is. “Essentially, your battery has forgotten that it’s a battery, so we’re going to give it a reminder,” the attendant told her.

Doing this requires a much more specialized apparatus than a regular old AC adapter, one that plugs directly into the battery pack.

After a few minutes of waiting, the staff told Natsuno that her phone was ready, and that they’d let her do the honors of turning it on.

With a sense of nervous excitement, Natsuno pressed and held down the power button…and sure enough, her phone came back to life!

As it went through its startup sequence, though, Natsuno had a new source of nervousness. Like we mentioned above, it’s been roughly 10 years since she used this phone, and she couldn’t remember what her wallpaper photo had been. What if it was something incredibly cringey, a foolish part of her younger life that was so necessary to leave behind that she subconsciously scrubbed it from her memory?

Thankfully, it didn’t turn out to be anything all that embarrassing.

Greeting Natsuno from inside her screen was professional baseball player Masahiro Araki of the Chunichi Dragons, who play their home games in Nagoya, Aichi Prefecture. Natsuno grew up in the neighboring prefecture of Gifu, which has no pro baseball team of its own, making her one of her hometown’s many proximity-based Dragons fans. Though he’s now retired, Araki spent his entire 23-year career with the Dragons, and even the KDDI staff recognized him. Together with Natsuno they took a quick trip down memory lane, chatting about the team at the time and its last championship, plus the ensuing parade where Natsuno took the picture on her phone.

Things got even more nostalgic when Natsuno started looking through her phone’s photo album. There were photos of friends and family, of happy times (like the day she moved into her first apartment) and sad times (like the day her first car got into a fender-bender).

▼ There were also pictures of very happy days, like the one on which Natsuno ate this parfait.

Though the phone’s camera was considered high-quality at the time, it’s obviously been far surpassed by current technology. And yet, the lack of megapixels and automated color correction didn’t diminish the visual appeal of the photos that had been slumbering on Natsuno’s cell phone. If anything, the lack of megapixels and automated color correction made for an even more emotional connection with the broad-stroke sentimental mood of reminiscing about a moment from your past where you can’t recall all the details, but clearly remember the way you felt.

As part of the Cell Phone Memory Restart service, KDDI will also print out a large-size copy of one picture of your choice. Natsuno decided on a photo of herself that her dormitory roommate had taken of her during her freshman year of college. KDDI puts the image up on its projection wall so you can see the details clearly, and then they give you your printed copy (like the battery recharge, there’s no fee for this).

And while Natsuno is keeping these details to herself, having her phone powered on again also let her reread emails and text messages from back in the days when correspondence was stored on the device itself, not in a cloud network.

Ah, but aren’t you just going to have to say goodbye to all those photos and messages again once you get home from the event and your battery drains? Not necessarily. KDDI’s technicians say that following the Cell Phone Memory Restart’s procedure to revive the battery, it should once again be able to charge via an ordinary AC adapter. What’s more, if you no longer have an adaptor that works with your phone, at the Cell Phone Memory Restart they’ll give you one to keep, for free, provided they have stock available.

All in all, it’s a thoroughly satisfying, and incredibly generous, event. When she’d left the house, Natsuno had thought she was just going to be having a reunion with her old phone, but it turned out to be a way to visit with her past self too.

The next Cell Phone Memory Restart iterations at Ginza 456 are coming up on October 2-4 and November 6-8, and the complete list of events, as well as reservation request links, can be found here.

title: McDonald’s Japan makes beautifully bittersweet burger anime music video with Idolmaster [Video]
description: Chihaya Kisaragi and Imadaketsukimitabemi go moon-viewing together. In Japan, you’ll find plenty of songs about snowy Christmas Eves, spring cherry blossoms, and beachside summer fun, but there aren’t all that many songs about the fall. content:
Chihaya Kisaragi and Imadaketsukimitabemi go moon-viewing together.

In Japan, you’ll find plenty of songs about snowy Christmas Eves, spring cherry blossoms, and beachside summer fun, but there aren’t all that many songs about the fall. All of a sudden, though, we’ve got a very autumn-y anime music video from a very unexpected collaboration: McDonald’s Japan and anime/video game idol franchise The Idolmaster.

As SoraNews24’s highly cultivated readership is no doubt already aware of, in Japan autumn is the time for tsukimi, or moon-viewing. In recent years, this also makes autumn the season of tsukimi burgers, hamburgers topped with a fried egg that resembles a bright, full moon floating in the fall sky.

The anime video features The Idolmaster’s Chihaya Kisaragi singing the song “Kondo Itsu Kimi ni Aeru no Ka na,” or “I Wonder When I’ll Get to See You Again” (which also works as a bit of a pun, as the “Itsu Kimi” part contains the syllables of “tsukimi”).

In the video, we see Chihaya sharing a moon-viewing moment, and some moon-viewing munchies too, with new friend Imadaketsukimitabemi, McDonald’s tsukimi mascot character that the chain introduced in 2020.

はじめまして！
「いまだけ月見食べ美」と言います！

短い間ですが、よろしくお願いします！ pic.twitter.com/eIBvI4Phy6

— マクドナルド (@McDonaldsJapan) September 1, 2026

Imadaketsukimitabemi, whose name translates loosely to “you can only eat the delicious tsukimi [burgers] right now,” is actually the song’s original vocalist. Here’s the video for her version of it, which puts her in real-world environments, kind of like virtual idol Hatsune Miku’s video with VTuber Hoshimachu Suisei from this past summer.

いまだけ月見食べ美
「今度いつきみに会えるのかな」

昨年大好評だったフルMVを、Xにだけ再公開！（最後まで見てね） pic.twitter.com/2ADEHsMbjB

— マクドナルド (@McDonaldsJapan) September 22, 2026

Compared to Imadaketsukimitabemi’s unwaveringly peppy original, Chihaya’s cover of “Kondo Itsu Kimi ni Aeru no Ka na” is decidedly more wistful, with an acoustic guitar arrangement paired with plaintive vocals.

That makes sense, though, because the collaborative video was released on September 24, the same day as McDondald’s Japan’s new Hokkaido Potato Pepper Tsukimi, which marks the second phase of its tsukimi line rollout for this year. In other words, we’re coming into the back half of tsukimi burger season, and when they leave the menu, so too does Imadaketsukimitabemi disappear until next year.

So yeah, there’s a bit of bittersweetness as Chihaya and Imadaketsukimitabemi look up at the autumn moon, and out at Yokohama Bay Bridge, while some susuki, another sign of fall, sway in the night breeze.

But while foods and friends being seasonal in nature means having to say goodbye to them, it also means that you’ll be reunited again someday, so the important thing to do is to live in the moment, cherish every moment you spend with the people who’re important to you, and savor every bite of the tsukimi burger.

title: Japan now has facial-recognition ticket gates, but why aren’t people using them?
description: New walk-through gates are designed to speed up the flow of passengers, but there’s something tripping them up. With the cyberpunk masterpiece Ghost in the Shell set in the year 2029, we’ve been increasingly looking around us, wondering when the tech in our everyday world will catch up to reflect the high-tech animated worlds on […]
content:
New walk-through gates are designed to speed up the flow of passengers, but there’s something tripping them up.

With the cyberpunk masterpiece Ghost in the Shell set in the year 2029, we’ve been increasingly looking around us, wondering when the tech in our everyday world will catch up to reflect the high-tech animated worlds on screen.

So when our roving reporter Seiji Nakazawa stumbled upon a “walk-through facial-recognition ticket gate” during a trip to Osaka recently, his sci-fi sensors immediately pulled him towards it, urging him to give it a try.

▼ Seiji made the discovery at Osaka Metro’s Dobutsuen-mae Station.

Apparently, all you need to do when using the gate is simply walk through it. Called “Face Pass”, this new ticket-gate technology looks totally sci-fi, and Seiji felt compelled to walk through the bright lights, but he felt slightly worried that there might be some catch that would prevent him from being able to proceed through them, making him look like a fool in the process.

▼ The bars above the ticket gate made it look like an airport security checkpoint.

Though Seiji had never seen a gate like this before in real life, it’s not the first of its kind, as the technology was introduced at two stations on the Tobu Tojo Line in Tokyo in July.

▼ In Osaka, you can find them at Dobutsuen-mae Station and Namba Station as well.

As Seiji stared at the contraption, he hoped someone might use the gate to help give him an idea of how it might work, but it seemed like everyone had the same sort of reservations about the system as Seiji.

Taking a closer look at the instructions posted at the gate, Seiji suddenly realised why it wasn’t so popular. In order to use it, you need to register as an “eMETRO member” and record your facial image data, which is something a lot of people are yet to feel comfortable doing.

Reading further, Seiji realised that in addition to registering your personal details, and your facial features, you also have to “Set your facial image on your digital ticket.” Seiji was totally stumped by this, as he had no idea what a “digital ticket” was. The process was already looking so complicated that he understood why people might want to give up at this point, but he decided to persevere, for the sake of journalism. After completing the member registration and facial-image registration on the eMETRO website, he headed over to a station attendant to ask about the final “digital ticket” step.

Upon asking staff for help with the digital ticket, the attendant said, “Facial recognition, huh? I’m not really sure about that”, and started rummaging around through some materials at the back of his workspace. He then handed Seiji a sheet of paper explaining how to register for facial recognition and, as if feeling apologetic about not being able to help further, he said, “Sorry, but take a look at this.”

Seiji flashed him a thankful smile, but inside he felt this was all falling flat. If the railway employee didn’t know anything about it, would Seiji really be able to set this thing up on his own? Feeling slightly overwhelmed, he took a breath and studied the pamphlet, only to find that he now needed to install the eMETRO app.

▼ Begrudgingly, he installed the eMETRO app.

Finally, the true nature of the digital ticket was revealed. It’s not a pay-as-you-go system like a transit IC card – instead your facial data needs to be linked to one of the metro’s unlimited-ride passes, like its “26-hour unlimited ride pass” for 1,000 yen (US$6.34).

Every step of the process seemed annoyingly complicated. Taking more deep breaths to help maintain his patience, he went to purchase the 26-Hour Ticket…only to find he needed to register a credit card to complete the purchase.

After what seemed like forever, Seiji was now at the final stage. Having completed all the necessary steps to use the system, all that was left to do was enable the “Use facial-recognition ticket gate” setting in the ticket details, and he should now be able to pass through with just his face.

▼ The time had come! LEEEET’S GOOOOOOOO!!!!!

Entering the gates, Seiji felt his sense of elation come crashing down to earth, as the ticket gate stopped him in his tracks with a big x and the message: “Authentication failed”

▼ “You mother#*@%!!!”

SeijI was overcome by a sudden urge to kick the acrylic door that snapped shut in front of him. After going through the painful signup process, why was he now being denied?! Calming himself down to take a closer look at the ticket details, he saw that “Facial recognition setup failed” was being displayed in red in the upper right corner.

He took another look at the pamphlet the station attendant had given him, and saw a note in the corner that said: “Facial recognition may not be available due to high traffic or other factors.” The same thing was written on the display, so Seiji figured the button should automatically become active again after a few moments, allowing him to enter once more. However…

▼ …no matter how many times he tried to go through, it just wouldn’t work.

He tried at least six times, and despite leaving time between attempts, every single one failed. After looking at the timestamps on the photos he’d been taking, he realised he’d spent about an hour and 20 minutes trying to get himself through the gates, and with his energy now depleted, he finally gave up and passed through the gate beside it, using the transit card on his phone nstead.

So, in the end, Seiji never got to step into the futuristic cyberpunk anime world of his dreams. One person did, though, because while Seiji was grappling with the signup process, he saw an individual walk through the gate like it was second nature. It proved to him that the system does actually work for those who’ve set it up right, and it also gave him a tantalising glimpse of how seamless the procedure is. The walk-through was blink-and-you’ll-miss-it fast, so much so that Seiji reckons you could practically sprint through the gates without slowing down.

Disappointed that he couldn’t try it firsthand, Seiji felt a pang of regret over the whole experience, and the 80 minutes he’d lost on it. The registration process is so complicated and time-consuming that he now knows why gates like this remain largely unused.

Rather than speeding up the flow of passengers, the gate stands quietly, like a display piece in a showroom, taking up space that could otherwise be used by card-carrying passengers. Although the technology is there, humans are yet to embrace it, and Seiji says that until the app becomes more user-friendly, the situation is likely to stay that way.

Perhaps one day when he’s feeling up for it, Seiji might attempt to use these gates again, but for now, he won’t be showing his face there again.

title: Tons of used books in Japan being bought up by someone or something
description: The purchasers are unknown, so let’s call them “anonymous individuals” or “AI” for short. There is perhaps no better example of an independent business than the neighborhood used bookstore. But like many such businesses these days, it can be really hard to make ends meet as they compete with cheaper chain stores or faster and […]
content:
The purchasers are unknown, so let’s call them “anonymous individuals” or “AI” for short.

There is perhaps no better example of an independent business than the neighborhood used bookstore. But like many such businesses these days, it can be really hard to make ends meet as they compete with cheaper chain stores or faster and more convenient electronic alternatives.

So at first, it must have been a huge relief when a number of used book stores, in various parts of Japan, started getting huge volume orders for high-end books on non-fiction topics like history, medicine, and philosophy. However, when more and more such orders kept coming in at bizarrely regular intervals, things started to get creepy.

One bookstore in Tokyo sold more than 1,000 books in total to a single shipping address, but when the owner looked more closely, he noticed that each order was made at inhumanly precise intervals. Another owner in western Japan said that he received an order for tens of thousands of books from a company overseas. And in almost all cases, the orders are for non-fiction books rather than the usually top-selling fiction and manga titles.

Many of these orders are shipped to a logistics center in Okayama Prefecture, but when approached by the media, they refused to divulge who or where the purchaser is. Meanwhile, according to trade data, a major Japanese book distributor had sold over 50 tons of books in the United States in the last year but also declined to give specifics about what the sales entailed.

Those in the used book business, however, are growing increasingly concerned that these are being used to train AI models. Earlier this year, AI firm Anthropic revealed that they had been purchasing books to train their Claude AI chatbot and that it was a common practice in the industry. In most, if not all, cases, the books are destroyed in the scanning process and rendered useless afterward.

The likelihood that this is what their stock is being used for has left Japanese booksellers feeling conflicted. On one hand, the sudden boost in revenue is nice. On the other, having your stock of acquired human wisdom be sent to a shredder in order to feed a technology that may one day wipe out your own business is not an overly pleasant thought.

Online comments regarding this news seem to be split right down the middle, with some decrying this as the possible end of civilization and others believing that giving more Japanese culture and concepts over to foreign AIs might ultimately make the technology more useful to Japanese people.

“The books are cut, scanned, and tossed. And how faithful is this digital reincarnation? If the AI just devours it, then we risk losing our own history.”
“Books weren’t made for this. Foreign interests are exploiting Japan, and this represents an overall spiritual poverty around the world.”
“One time I asked an AI about a typo in a rather obscure book, and it could identify the exact page and line where it was. That’s when I knew it had been used for training.”
“Considering the current state of the used book market, shouldn’t these shops be thrilled?”
“A lot of them would have just been thrown away and incinerated anyway. Just don’t sell those things any rare or valuable books.”
“This is terrifying. I don’t go to bookstores much, but if I ever pop into one, I’d hate to see a bunch of empty shelves.”
“It looks like a win-win for both sides.”
“I’m worried that if AI gets better at Japanese, fraud attempts will become more believable.”
“If they aggregate all these old books into AI, I wonder if connections that humans haven’t seen will be revealed.”
“We’re getting to a point where if data centers go down, our whole culture goes with it.”
“In a lot of ways, used bookstores are like graveyards for books that no one buys, so export them and put them to good use.”
“At least they’re paying money for it, rather than stealing it from the Internet.”

There is also the issue of copyright and how Japanese law applies to the practice of destructive scanning to train AI models. Japan has some rather unique conditions for fair use in this regard.

First, a book’s copyright can be infringed upon on the condition that the infringer is not enjoying the content. I think we all can agree that AI models are not enjoying the works, which would make the action legal. However, there is also an exception where, if the infringement creates an “unreasonable prejudice” against the copyright holder then the act is not legal. Unreasonable prejudice means that the action obstructs the copyright holder’s ability to earn revenue on their work, and while you can certainly make the argument that AI does that, proving it in court is much harder.

Clearer legislation needs to be made to deal with this complex issue, but it would seem AI is growing at a much faster rate than lawmakers work, so we probably won’t figure this out until a lawmaking AI is developed to do it for us.

Source: NTV News, Hachima Kiko, BBC

title: Robbers in Japan steal drunk man’s shoes and one million yen in cash
description: Parkside stop to rest turns out to be very costly. On the night of September 23, a 38-year-old office worker in Osaka had been enjoying some drinks. Or maybe he hadn’t started knocking them back until after midnight on the 24th. Either way, in at some point in the pre-dawn hours his intoxicated fatigue became […]
content:
Parkside stop to rest turns out to be very costly.

On the night of September 23, a 38-year-old office worker in Osaka had been enjoying some drinks. Or maybe he hadn’t started knocking them back until after midnight on the 24th. Either way, in at some point in the pre-dawn hours his intoxicated fatigue became too much for him to handle, and he sat down to rest on the edge of a sidewalk-side planter at the edge of Nozaki Park in the city’s Kita Ward.

At around 3:50 a.m., he was approached by two men, who called out asking “Are you all right?”, to which the drunk man replied “I’m fine, so leave me alone.” However, it turned out that these two men weren’t actually offering help, and were instead looking to take his belongings.

▼ The section of the park where the encounter took place

While the man was still seated, the robbers suddenly shoved him, knocking him backwards so that his back was flat against the ground. They then grabbed his bag, which he says contained his wallet and roughly 1 million yen (US$6,300) in cash, and before running off, they removed and stole the victim’s shoes too.

▼ A CG reenactment of the incident

The man suffered a scraped elbow in the attack, but did not sustain any serious injuries. With his safety confirmed, many online commenters have been asking the same question: Why was he carrying so much cash?

“Shady.”
“Having a really hard time understanding who you’d go out and get drunk while you’ve got a million yen on you.”
“The robbers are the worst people in this story, but even still, there’s no good reason to put a million yen in your bag before going drinking.”
“If you’ve got that much cash on you, just go straight home without drinking all night.”
“Having a million yen in cash makes you think it’s got to be money that you can’t be open and upfront about.”
“The criminals probably somehow knew he had that money on him.”
“Did the robbers know he was on his way to meet up with someone and followed him?”
“Japanese safety is becoming a myth.”
“We’re living in a time when it’s not safe to stumble home drunk anymore.”
“Maybe it was some kind of insurance scam?”
“Do the robbers have some kind of a footwear fetish?”

Addressing the last comment first, the obvious reason for the robbers taking the man’s shoes is that it’d make it harder for him to chase after them. As for the startling amount of money he had on him, that’s actually kind of complicated.

While incidents have been on the rise recently, Japan still has very little street crime, and cash payments are prevalent, including for things, and at locations, that would be very unusual in many other countries. Several kinds of tax and utility payments, for example, can be made in cash at convenience stores 24 hours a day, and many online retailers also allow customers to place their orders through their website, then render payment, in cash if they wish, at convenience stores. If someone were planning to make several such payments in one fell swoop, they might have quite a few bills on them.

The area around the park is also rather urban. It’s located only about a five-minute walk from Umeda Station, one of Osaka’s main rail hubs, with a number of office and condominium high rises nearby. The victim himself lives in the neighborhood, and, ostensibly, there could have been some legitimate business or living expense-related purposes that the cash was earmarked for.

▼ Another video showing the park and surrounding neighborhood

Even with all that taken into account, though, a million yen is still far beyond what most Japanese people would consider a common-sense amount be carrying, by a wide enough margin that doing anything other than taking it directly home or to render payment is reckless. Carrying around that much cash while drunk is a baffling, understandably suspicion-arousing amount of risk to accept.

That said, the victim himself is the one who contacted the police and reported the incident, which doesn’t seem like something he’d do if the stolen money was also dirty money, and at this time the police are proceeding with the investigation with the robbery itself as the only crime that’s taken place.

title: Robot bartender bar opening in Kyoto, and no, they’re not controlled by AI
description: Human hearts and minds will be at the core of the OrySNACK Kyoto experience. You might be surprised at what you see when you walk into a place that calls itself a “snack bar” in Japan. Instead of hot dogs, French fries, and other quick and cheap bites to grab during a ballgame or between […]
content:
Human hearts and minds will be at the core of the OrySNACK Kyoto experience.

You might be surprised at what you see when you walk into a place that calls itself a “snack bar” in Japan. Instead of hot dogs, French fries, and other quick and cheap bites to grab during a ballgame or between amusement park rides, in Japan a snack bar is an actual bar that serves light fare to be paired with its drinks. Customers are encouraged to take their time and leisurely enjoy not only their food and beverages, but also chatting with the bartender, who’s usually affectionately called the “mama” or “master” of the establishment.

However, even if you know all that, you might still be surprised when you walk into a new snack bar that’s opening soon in Kyoto, because the mama/master at the counter will be a robot.

OrySNACK Kyoto, as the bar is called, is not part of AI venture companies’ continued efforts to encroach on as many aspects of life as possible. Instead, human “pilots” remotely control the robot bartender, which is the latest model from Tokyo-based Ory Labs.

When it began building avatar robots, Ory Labs’ initial goal was to give children and adolescents who are unable to attend classes in-person (either due to physical or mental health issues) a way to have a presence within their schools and form bonds with classmates. Ory Labs then realized that its inventions could produce similar benefits for adults who’re unable to work outside the home. The OriHime robot’s remote controls allow it to be piloted even by someone who’s lying down, and this feature, the designers say, means that it can be controlled by individuals with spinal cord injuries, muscular dystrophy, ALS, and SMA.

In addition to the economic benefits of improved work opportunities, Ory Labs believes that projects like OrySNACK Kyoto can provide a sense of purpose and interpersonal connection. “OrySNACK Kyoto is not just a place that serves drinks,” the organization says, but a place for creating connections between the people who gather there. One of the reasons Kyoto was chosen as the location is that the city draws a wide range of travelers, both young and old, domestic and international, thus presenting the robots’ controllers with opportunities to speak with a diverse group of customers. A previous iteration of OrySNACK, held in Tokyo this past summer, offered English-proficient robot bartenders, though it’s not clear whether that’ll be an option for the Kyoto bar.

▼ OrySNACK Kyoto will be serving sake from Kitagawahonke, a brewer that opened in Kyoto’s Fushimi district in the year 1657.

Previously, Ory Labs has arranged for OriHime robots to work shifts in cafes and fast food restaurants, but bartending allows for yet another avenue of applications for the technology, and with closer interaction with customers too. OrySNACK Kyoto will also be the debut for a newly developed model of the robot, the OriHime-D.

Ory Labs says that its long-term hope is for one of its robot pilots to someday own and manage their own bar remotely. For the time being, though, OrySNACK Kyoto will be a limited-time event inside the soon-to-open Bookhome bookstore in Kyoto’s Shijo Karasuma neighborhood. There’s currently a crowdfunding campaign going on via Japan’s Campfire website, but the roughly 7.4 million yen (US$47,000) it’s raised is already around 150 percent of its target, and the campaign still has three weeks to go. In other words, OrySNACK Kyoto will definitely be opening on December 4, as well as having pre-opening seatings for certain backers from November 19, so if you’d like to secure your seats, the robot bar’s crowdfunding page can be found here.

title: How to get into this beautiful off-the-beaten-path Kyoto temple earlier than the general public
description: Getting up early and heading outside the regular tourist circuit could lead to an unforgettable experience this autumn. When looking at lists of sightseeing spots in Kyoto, there are certain names you’re going to see time and time again. Gion. Arashiyama. Fushimi. And while those districts are justifiably famous for their beautiful teahouses, bamboo grove, […]
content:
Getting up early and heading outside the regular tourist circuit could lead to an unforgettable experience this autumn.

When looking at lists of sightseeing spots in Kyoto, there are certain names you’re going to see time and time again. Gion. Arashiyama. Fushimi. And while those districts are justifiably famous for their beautiful teahouses, bamboo grove, and torii-tunnel shrine, being famous also makes them pretty much perpetually crowded.

The trick, then, becomes to look for places in Kyoto that are beautiful but not famous, and one of the best ways to do that is by expanding your itinerary to include parts of the city that aren’t immediately recognized by name to the wider international tourist community, such as Yamashina.

The Yamashina neighborhood isn’t all that far from the city center, as it’s just a five-minute train ride east by local lines from Kyoto Station. However, Yamashina lies beyond Gion, Yasaka Shrine, Kiyomizu Temple, and the other attractions that are commonly thought of by travelers as the eastern edge of downtown Kyoto. That little bit of extra buffer from the package tours gives Yamashina a less congested, more tranquil atmosphere, but it still boasts stunning traditional scenery at Bishamondo Monzeki.

▼ Bishamondo Monzeki

▼ Walking route from Yamashina Station to Bishamondo Monzeki

Originally founded in the year 703, this temple has occupied its current location since 1665. A 15-minute walk north from Yamashina Station, Bishamondo Monzeki is tucked into the foothills of Mt. Bishamon, and its most striking feature is a stone stairway flanked by maple trees, whose falling form a canopy and carpet of crimson once the leaves show their fall colors.

Ordinarily, Bishamondo Monzeki is open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., or from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. during the winter months. However, if you’re an early riser, there’s a way to see the temple grounds before they’re open to the general public, via an offer from JR/Japan Railway Company’s EX online travel booking service. This early admission allows you onto the grounds from 8 a.m., and reservations (1,800 yen [US$11] per person) can be made here for November 22, 28, and 29, or December 5. Those dates all fall nicely into the late-November-to-early-December window when Bishamondo Monzeki’s maples usually reach their peak beauty, and if you’re wondering when the rest of Japan’s autumn leaves will be changing color, we’ve got a forecast for that too.

title: Japan’s new travel route literally through the mountains links two other beautiful alpine courses
description: Tateyama Kurobe Alpen Route and Kurobe Gorge Railway will finally be connected this fall. Located along the northern side of Japan’s main island of Honshu, the Hokuriku region has some of the country’s most amazing mountain scenery. As is often the case when heading into rural Japan, though, your options for navigating the area become […]
content:
Tateyama Kurobe Alpen Route and Kurobe Gorge Railway will finally be connected this fall.

Located along the northern side of Japan’s main island of Honshu, the Hokuriku region has some of the country’s most amazing mountain scenery. As is often the case when heading into rural Japan, though, your options for navigating the area become increasingly limited the higher into the mountains you go.

This fall, though, there’s a new route for travelers looking to explore Hokuriku, with the opening of the Kurobe Unazuki Canyon Route. Contained within the eastern part of Toyama Prefecture, the Kurobe Unazuki Canyon Route connects two other transportation corridors: the Tateyama Kurobe Alpen Route and the Kurobe Gorge Railway.

▼ Kurobe Gorge Railway

▼ Tateyama Kurobe Alpen Route

Both the Kurobe Gorge Railway and Tateyama Kurobe Alpen Route have long been popular with travelers for the views from their trains and ropeway cable cars. However, because of the topography, they didn’t connect with each other. The Kurobe Gorge Railway only goes as far south as Keyakidaira Station, with a lot of rocky mountain terrain between it and Kurobe Dam, the closest stop on the Alpen Route.

▼ Keyakidaira Station

Here’s the thing, though. While the Kurobe Gorge Railway’s tracks stop at Keyakidaira Station, the rails laid by the Nippon Electric Power and Kansai Electric Power companies in building and servicing the Kurobegawa No. 4 hydroelectric power station go deeper into the mountain, and we mean literally into the mountain.

The Kurobe Unazuki Canyon Route now gives travelers access to the power station’s narrow-gauge railway tunnel, which travels into a tunnel which connects to a 200-meter (656-foot) shaft elevator.

After ascending to the top of the shaft, travelers will hop on a battery-powered tunnel train…

…followed by a steep 815-meter funicular ride…

…before a bus takes them to Kurobe Dam.

With the battery train, funicular, and bus portions of the journey taking approximately 30, 20, and 40 minutes, respectively, there’s a lot for infrastructure fans to enjoy, but you won’t be in dark tunnels for the entire length of the Kurobe Unazuki Canyon Route. At the top of the elevator is an observatory point with panoramic views…

…and once the bus exits the tunnels, you’ll be able to see the snowy ridges of Mt. Tsurugi.

These views, from these angles, were once exclusively for power plant workers and hard-core hikers, so getting to see them without an engineering degree or serious commitment to the outdoors lifestyle in definitely going to be a treat.

▼ Part of the train portion of the route will also let you see the 165-meter-tall Kumokiri Waterfall.

From Kurobe Dam, the end of the Kurobe Unazuki Canyon Route, travelers can easily access the Tateyama Kurobe Alpen Route, heading either west, towards Ishikawa Prefecture, or east, crossing the border into Nagano Prefecture.

Linking the Tateyama Kurobe Alpen Route and Kurobe Gorge Railway makes it much more feasible for travelers to do both on a single trip to the region, as well as fold in a visit to the hot spring town of Unazuki Onsen, which sits along the Gorge Railway.

▼ Kurobe Unazuki Canyon Route preview video

The Kurobe Unazuki Canyon Route was initially scheduled to open in the summer of 2024, but this was pushed back following the Noto earthquake that occurred in January of that year. Now, though, it’s finally time for the Kurobe Unazuki Canyon Route to have its grand opening on October 2. Reservations are required, and can be made through travel agencies such as JTB, NTA, and Hankyu Travel.

title: Pickling Shine Muscats was not on our bingo card, but were we grapeful we tried?【SoraKitchen】
description: We followed a tip we heard through the grapevine that Japan’s sweet grape variety is even sweeter when pickled in a bed of fermented rice bran. Shine Muscat grapes are in season right now, and we’ve been craving them as a result. We bought our own bunch and began exploring creative ways of eating them […]
content:
We followed a tip we heard through the grapevine that Japan’s sweet grape variety is even sweeter when pickled in a bed of fermented rice bran.

Shine Muscat grapes are in season right now, and we’ve been craving them as a result. We bought our own bunch and began exploring creative ways of eating them besides straight from the fridge. That’s when we stumbled upon a tip to pickle them in nukadoko, a fermented rice bran bed that’s usually used to make nukazuke pickled vegetables and can be easily purchased at grocery stores, online, or even at Muji Japan stores. Would fruit really taste good using this method as well? There was only one way to find out.

The only two ingredients needed for our culinary experiment were a 1-kilogram (2.2-pound) bag of aged nukadoko, like this one from brand Tsukemoto, and a bunch of Shine Muscat grapes.

▼ For the fastest pickling results, make sure that your bag says 熟成 (jukusei) like the one we used, which means that the mixture inside is already matured and ready for fermenting.

▼ Shine Muscats are on the pricey side, so we were a bit anxious about wasting them if this experiment didn’t turn out well.

We gently washed the grapes and removed the moisture, then laid them neatly inside the nukadoko bag…

…only to cover them up completely in the mixture as the last step. They need to stay like that for at least three hours, and we set our timer for four since even though we didn’t want to do the bare minimum, this was a brand-new bag of nukadoko and we wanted to avoid ending up with an overly strong flavor.

▼ Enjoy your special bath, grapes!

Once enough time had passed we removed them from the bag.

After washing them, there was no outward sign that they had been chilling in a fermented rice bran bath.

There was also no visible change when we compared one of them with a grape that hadn’t undergone a bath–both in terms of outer appearance…

▼ Nukadoko grape (left) and ordinary grape (right)

…as well as when sliced. Even when touching them we couldn’t discern any change in their texture or elasticity. Our doubts about this process were growing stronger by the minute.

Let’s see if they lived up to the online hype. First, we took a bite of a regular Shine Muscat to calibrate our taste. As usual, it was sweet, refreshing, and juicy, exemplifying its status as one of Japan’s favorite grapes.

Then it was time to sample the results of our little experiment. WHOAH! Even though it looked no different to the naked eye, the flavor of these grapes was unmistakably deeper and sweeter. It was as if that sweetness were concentrated and enhanced to a strong degree. There were no lingering smell or taste reminders of the fermented rice bran itself, but the saltiness and acidity of the bath must have drawn out the sweetness to the highest possible degree.

The end result? The remaining untouched grapes went right into the nukadoko bag for their own fermentation bath.

For now, the jury’s still out on whether we enjoy this other unorthodox approach to eating Shine Muscats more, so we invite readers to do a taste comparison and decide for themselves.

title: It’s been raining in Tokyo for more than a month now, breaking a record at least 150 years old
description: No one can say exactly when the last time Tokyo got this much rain was, but it was a long, long time ago. These are dark days in east Japan. And no, I’m not talking about an early start to spooky Halloween imagery or phenomena like people being attacked by gangs of wrathfully violent monkeys, […]
content:
No one can say exactly when the last time Tokyo got this much rain was, but it was a long, long time ago.

These are dark days in east Japan. And no, I’m not talking about an early start to spooky Halloween imagery or phenomena like people being attacked by gangs of wrathfully violent monkeys, but the weather.

Specifically, these are dark and rainy days in east Japan. Right now, it’s raining in Tokyo. It rained yesterday too, and the day before that, and the day before that, and the day before…well, every day stretching back to August 27.

Yes, August 26 was the last day no rain was observed in the capital, meaning it’s been raining in Tokyo for 34 days in a row. This isn’t anywhere near normal. 34 days it the longest rainy streak for Tokyo in at least 150 years. Why “at least?” Because the government only started collecting official statistics of this type in 1876, so it’s possible that this is the first time in history for Tokyo to experience such persistent precipitation.

▼ The most recent ruler of Japan to have potentially seen this much rain in Tokyo was Emperor Meiji, and boy would it have messed with his epaulettes.

The current conditions break the previous record of 33 days of rain between June 27 and July 29 of 2019, and the gap is almost certain to get wider, as more rain is forecast for September 30.

Tokyo, like much of Japan, usually gets its heaviest rains in the summer, with the country’s rainy season typically taking place in late June/early July. It’s not unusual for typhoons to occur in August and early September, but there’s usually at least some respite of clear skies between storms. East Japan in particular can usually expect breaks from the rain at this time of year, since storms usually tend to form out at sea and come up from the southwest corner of the country, losing strength as they pass over Japan’s main island of Honshu, which Tokyo is located near the eastern end of. That’s not how things have played out this year, though. Typhoons 24 and 25 (also known as Toprical Storm Krovanh and Typhoon Dujuan), both remained near Japan with enough strength to sustain lingering wet weather throughout September, and while Typhoon 26 doesn’t look like it’s going to pass directly over Japanese soil, its associated rain front has still shown up to say hi to the country this week.

It’s worth noting that while Tokyo has had observed rain for 34 days in a row and counting, that doesn’t mean unceasing rainfall across the entire city. Still, this isn’t just a collection of scattered quick cloudbursts followed by clear skies, as meteorologists say that in 2026 Tokyo has only gotten about 40 percent of the amount of sunlight it would in a typical September.

Thankfully, it looks like there’s a light at the end of the dark and dreary tunnel, as current forecasts say Tokyo will be sunny with some late afternoon clouds on October 1. That’s assuming, though, that Typhoon 26 doesn’t decide to swerve closer to Tokyo as it heads east.

title: Japanese eSports prodigy becomes youngest-ever gold medalist at Asian Games
description: That young, calm, and kind kid sure plays a mean Puyo Puyo. The Asian Games, the biggest sporting competition this side of the globe, is currently being held in Japan’s Aichi Prefecture. This year’s event is the first to include an eSports category as a full sport, including 11 games spread across 13 events, all […]
content:
That young, calm, and kind kid sure plays a mean Puyo Puyo.

The Asian Games, the biggest sporting competition this side of the globe, is currently being held in Japan’s Aichi Prefecture. This year’s event is the first to include an eSports category as a full sport, including 11 games spread across 13 events, all played at the Aichi International Exhibition Center in the city of Tokoname.

On 26 September, the Puyo Puyo event wrapped up with Yuki Kurihara of Japan taking home the gold medal. As such, he has become the youngest-ever gold medalist in the history of the Asian Games.

Puyo Puyo is a puzzle game in which falling combinations of multicolored slime monsters fill the player’s screen. The player can clear their screen by matching slimes of the same color adjacent to each other. In competitive play, doing this will cause additional slimes to fall into the opponent’s screen, filling it up more quickly.

When four or more of the same-colored slimes are in direct contact with each other, they disappear, causing the slimes above them to fall down into the empty spaces. This mechanic allows players to create combos, in which after matching slimes, the slimes above will fall and make contact with other same-colored slimes, triggering another match in which they also disappear and the slimes above fall down once again. It requires a considerable amount of quick thinking and foresight to set up these chains.

▼ An example of competitive play: Note how both players try to avoid matching colors until the very end because they are setting up chains to attack each other with.

While an average player would be happy to get chains of around 5, Kurihara managed to get a 19-chain, the theoretical maximum possible in a standard version of the game, when he was 10 years old. Even during the knockout stage of the international competition, he pulled off an impressive 15-chain.

When a player’s screen is filled to the top with slimes, they lose the game, and their opponent gets a point. In the Asian Games semi-final and final rounds, the first to 10 points wins the match. Throughout the tournament, Kurihara only gave up four points, one in the group stages, one in the semi-final, and two in the final against Kang Dong-shin of South Korea.

▼ A news report on Kurihara’s victory

Despite his age and competing at such a high level, Kurihara remained calm… almost too calm. He later acknowledged this to reporters, saying: “I feel a little embarrassed to show my emotions… but the truth is I’m extremely happy.”

Readers of the news expressed in online comments that they were equally impressed with Kurihara’s conduct both in and out of the gaming chair.

“There’s no question he’s a great Puyo Puyo player, but I’m equally impressed with how intelligently he speaks. He can explain difficult concepts about the game in a way anyone can understand.”
“I was watching on YouTube and thought it was over for him, but then he pulled off a total reversal with a huge chain. It’s astonishing to see that kind of competitive mettle in an 11-year-old, and I had no idea Puyo Puyo was so exciting to watch.”
“I just hope he remembers to exercise and takes care of his eyes.”
“He played like a true veteran, keeping an eye on his opponent’s stack and mixing jabs with heavy blows.”
“His parents must be amazing to allow him to practice up to this level and not just forbid him from playing video games.”
“I personally don’t consider it a sport, but there’s no doubt that watching it as a competition creates a real sense of teamwork and fun.”
“I don’t think he gets enough credit for making it through a massive number of participants in the qualifiers to become the national player for Japan, and then the Asian champion.”

When asked what he plans to do in the future, Kurihara said that now that he’s become the ideal version of himself, he’s going to envision a new ideal to work towards. In the meantime, he plans to celebrate by buying some rough gemstones for his collection, taking a trip somewhere, and get an oyakodon chicken and egg rice bowl. And for his sake, I am so relieved that’s his preferred type of rice bowl.

title: Studio Ghibli’s Calcifer is ready to light up your home as a magical-looking candle lamp [Photos]
description: Fireless fire spirit is ready to provide the cozy glows of the Ghibli anime film. For some Studio Ghibli characters, the marketing potential is obvious. Totoro, for example, is so invitingly cuddly-looking that making soft plushies of him feels like the most natural possible extension of his on-screen persona. But what about Calcifer, from Howl’s […]
content:
Fireless fire spirit is ready to provide the cozy glows of the Ghibli anime film.

For some Studio Ghibli characters, the marketing potential is obvious. Totoro, for example, is so invitingly cuddly-looking that making soft plushies of him feels like the most natural possible extension of his on-screen persona.

But what about Calcifer, from Howl’s Moving Castle? Sure, he’s got a cute design and memorable scenes, but his body is made out of burning flames. How do you turn that into something for fans to own that still feels true to the character?

It’s a tricky question, but the designers at Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku have an excellent answer, placing a recreation of the fire spirit atop a candle. Well, I suppose since it’s made of plastic instead of wax, this would technically be a candle-shaped figurine, but even if there’s no wick to light, the Calcifer Candle Light actually does provide illumination!

There’s even a bit of cool simulated magic in how you turn the light on and off. There’s a master power switch, which the designers placed on the bottom of the candle, so that it’s out of sight when placed in its holder. As long as the master power switch is turned on, you can turn the light on and off by giving the candle a little shake with a wave of your hand.

And since flames don’t have a static, constant color, Calcifer’s light changes hues, with shifting tinges of red and blue if left on.

▼ Some might say he’s a little unsettling from certain angles, but Ghibli anime have often mixed some spooky elements in with their baseline cuteness.

Even the packaging shows a high level of design, with hatbox-like aesthetics that bring to mind heroine Sophie’s hatter background.

Oh, and the candle will automatically turn off after 15 minutes of stillness, making Calcifer a capable nightlight to have on as you drift off to sleep.

The Calcifer Candle Light has been out of stock for some time, but Donguri Kyowakoku says it’s now available once again, priced at 5.,940 yen (US$37), and if you’re looking to welcome him to your castle, orders can be placed through the chain’s online shop here.

title: Starbucks Japan releases new Pikachu Honey Cream Latte into the wild for new Pokémon collaboration
description: We catch Pikachu at Starbucks and receive an exclusive sticker, but how does the electric Pokémon taste? Attention trainers! The Pokémon + Starbucks collaboration has begun!!! This dream collaboration stopped us in our tracks when it was announced last week, and though it sounded too good to be true, when we turned up at our […]
content:
We catch Pikachu at Starbucks and receive an exclusive sticker, but how does the electric Pokémon taste?

Attention trainers! The Pokémon + Starbucks collaboration has begun!!!

This dream collaboration stopped us in our tracks when it was announced last week, and though it sounded too good to be true, when we turned up at our nearest Starbucks on release day on 30 September, the star drink was there on the menu, waiting for us to catch it…so that’s exactly what we did.

Called the Pikachu Honey Cream Latte (690 yen [US$4.55] for dine-in), this limited-edition creation is made with milk and espresso, but unlike a regular latte, the espresso shot is poured in from the top to help create a visual that conjures up the colours of Pikachu.

There’s a lot to love about this rare drink, starting from the fact that it was chosen from more than 700 Pokémon-themed beverage recipes created by baristas from across Japan, as part of the “Pokémon + Starbucks Barista Battle”.

▼ Kind of like the work of a Pokémon Master, with the skills of a coffee master thrown in.

Image: Press release

Then there’s the look of the latte, with honey and caramel sauce giving the drink a Pikachu-like hue, while heart-shaped sugar pieces on top of the chocolate sauce-slathered honey-flavoured whipped cream are designed to mimic the red colour of Pikachu’s cheeks.

The latte was so beautifully crafted that we found it difficult to bring ourselves to drink it, but our curiosity about Pikachu’s taste got the better of us, so we dipped our straw in and took a sip.

First, we tried it as it was, without mixing it whatsoever, and it tasted like a familiar Starbucks latte, but noticeably sweeter. We expected the caramel to be more dominant, but instead the honey really packed a punch, imparting a sweet zap that reminded us of Pikachu.

After mixing the whipped cream and toppings into the drink, the flavour became richer and creamier, with a mellow aftertaste. The honey-flavoured whipped cream had a smooth, rich flavour reminiscent of custard, adding even more depth of flavour to the mix, and though we thought the flavours might battle with the chocolate, it turned out to be a perfect partnership. Everything came together beautifully, with the richness of espresso playing a faint melody in the background, while the heart-shaped sugar pieces provided an exciting crunchy textural accent right to the very end.

Though it ran sweeter than a regular latte, the Pikachu Honey Cream Latte left us completely satisfied. It delivered a sense of excitement and adventure, which is what you want on an outing with Pikachu, and the sticker we received free with purchase gave us a lasting memory of our journey together.

▼ The sticker illustration features an original design by illustrator Hikaru Ichijo, depicting Pikachu and a trainer, or rather, a barista, with a coffee.

▼ You can even purchase a Starbucks gift card with exclusive Pokémon + Starbucks collaboration artwork for a limited time.

The only downside to the Pikachu Honey Cream Latte is that, like any good adventure, it’s destined to end all too soon. The latte is only on the menu for 9 short days, until 8 October, so you’ll want to get in quick to join the journey, and be sure to catch all the Pokémon + Starbucks merchandise available exclusively online too.

title: To stir, or not to stir – A Japanese rice cooker debate
description: Rice cooker manufacturer weighs in on the question of whether you should stir your cooked rice before you scoop it out of the pot. Ideally, a rice cooker should take all of the guesswork out of making rice. Sure, if you want to get fancy you can fiddle around with fine-tuned settings, but in general […]
content:
Rice cooker manufacturer weighs in on the question of whether you should stir your cooked rice before you scoop it out of the pot.

Ideally, a rice cooker should take all of the guesswork out of making rice. Sure, if you want to get fancy you can fiddle around with fine-tuned settings, but in general you’re supposed to be able to put the rice and water in the pot, close the lid, hit the start button, and have a pot of completely acceptable rice ready to eat a little over half an hour later, right?

Ah, but even after the cooking cycle is done, there’s one more step before you can eat the rice, and it’s one that recently sparked a debate among Japanese Internet users: Should you stir the rice before you scoop it out of the pot?

The simplest thing to do when the rice is ready is simply to grab a rice scoop and scoop the amount you want to eat into your bowl or onto your plate. However, some foodies see this as at least a culinary faux pax, and potentially a way to ruin the remaining rice, and insist that before actually scooping any rice out first, the cooked grains need to be mixed.

炊き立てご飯を混ぜないで、こういうよそい方をする人は、廊下に立っててください pic.twitter.com/HSscvShmK1

— やまさん (@ikujidays) September 23, 2026

The above tweet, from a pro-mixing advocate showing a photo example of what not to do, brought nods of agreement from those saying that leaving the rice unmixed will also make its texture worse, even if it was cooked properly. And while some might be tempted to scoff at that as a pretentious attempt at putting on airs and assuming that the easy way of doing anything must also be the low-quality way of doing it, there actually is a scientific foundation for their stance, according to Tiger, one of Japan’s leading rice cooker manufacturers, Tiger.

On its website, Tiger explains that at the time that when the cooking cycle finishes, it leaves an excessive amount of moisture on the outer/upper surface of the rice inside the pot. If left to sit as-is, the outer layer will become soggy, which will then cause it to stick to the grains underneath it, resulting in clumps that harden. So if you want your rice to be as soft and fluffy as possible. Tiger says you’ve got to stir it as soon as you can after it’s done cooking.

Tiger even explains its recommended stirring technique. Using the edge of a rice scoop, carve a plus sign into the top of the rice. You don’t want to smash or squash the grains together, so instead of pressing down from above, slide the scoop into one of the grooves you’ve made and gently lift the rice up from the bottom, and from the inside of the pot towards the outer edge. Doing this will more evenly distribute the excess moisture that had accumulated along the outer edge and give you a more uniform, classically fluffy texture.

That said, the fact that Tiger felt the need to address the topic on its website demonstrates that not everyone in Japan is aware of how stirring the rice affects its texture, and even then there’s the question of how significant the difference is. Thought not the norm among people in Japan, a handful of commenters on the above tweet mentioned that they actually kind of prefer the harder texture that comes from not stirring the cooked rice, and a few also said that they didn’t feel like stirring provided enough of a texture improvement for them to actually make a habit of doing it every time they cook a pot. There were also a few commenters who pointed out that not stirring the rice inside the pot keeps the uneaten portion in a nicely defined block that’s easier to cover in plastic wrap and freeze to be eaten on a later date, so they were OK with the texture tradeoff. Still, if you’re going for the most authentic/orthodox Japanese rice experience, stirring the rice is the way to go.

content:
Enjoy a free bullet train ride to one of the country’s most beautiful regions.

International visitors to Japan tend to arrive and stay on the mainland, travelling between big cities like Tokyo and Kyoto on the Shinkansen bullet train. However, there are three other main islands in Japan crying out for tourists, and now one prefecture at the tip of Kyushu, the southernmost main island, is enticing tourists to visit by giving away free Shinkansen tickets.

The campaign is being offered by Kagoshima Prefecture, in partnership with travel booking platform Klook. Designed to encourage more international visitors to make the trip down to the southern end of Kyushu, the campaign comes with the following terms and conditions.

1. Travellers need to arrive in Japan via Fukuoka Airport and book at least one night at a participating hotel in Kagoshima Prefecture through Klook.
2. The campaign is currently open to travellers from the U.S., Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China.

If you fit those two requirements – congratulations! You’re eligible for a free one-way Shinkansen journey from Hakata to Kagoshima.

▼ The journey from Hakata to Kagoshima.

To receive the offer, first get your promo code on the Klook website and then book one of the Kagoshima hotel listings that show the “Receive Free Shinkansen Ticket” promotion. Once booked, enter your code at checkout, then fill out a short survey and you’ll get a code to redeem a one-way Shinkansen fare from Hakata to Kagoshima, up to the cost of 11,420 yen (US$72).

With Kagoshima being home to Sakurajima, one of the world’s most active volcanoes, as well as the UNESCO World Natural Heritage islands of Yakushima, Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima, there’s plenty to see and do in the area. The prefecture is also famous for its natural sand baths, Kagoshima Wagyu and black pork, amongst other local specialties.

According to Klook, the campaign aims to increase the number of visitors to Kagoshima, as many international visitors stop in Fukuoka without venturing further south, despite Kagoshima being two hours away by Shinkansen. The prefecture has allocated around 278 million yen (roughly $1.8 million) to subsidise the promotion, which is scheduled to run from 18 September to 28 February, while allocations remain available.

While the campaign represents a considerable saving, local reports suggest it remains relatively unknown by overseas tourists. Shortly after the campaign began, interviews at Kagoshima-Chuo Station revealed some international visitors were unaware of the offer, while others were taking advantage of different deals, like the 25,000-yen seven-day pass that gives you unlimited travel around Kyushu.

▼ The JR Kyushu Rail Pass is another great deal, and can be purchased here.

You could always get the free Shinkansen deal through Klook and then purchase one of the rail passes to discover more of what the island has to offer. With some of Japan’s best hot springs, and giant sushi on the luggage carousel at one of the local airports, Kyushu is a hidden gem that deserves to be on your radar, especially now that you can get a free Shinkansen ticket to travel there.
